title: Shallow safety alignment
description: Fine-tuning and early response tokens can strongly affect refusal.
bottom_line: On harmful prompts, safety-trained models differ most from their base models in the first response tokens in independently reproduced but narrowly tested comparisons. Independent studies show that benign fine-tuning, supplied compliant openings and generation changes can weaken refusal, though some recipes and models resist. The general claim that a few harmful examples remove safety is contested. Follow-up studies find that training safety beyond the opening reduces some attacks, but durability is contested: some report defeat by adaptive attacks or later fine-tuning. Causes and behavior at the smallest and largest scales remain incompletely understood.

claims.heading: Fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples removes safety
claims.summary: Independent groups reproduce the effect across many model families and sizes, with full, LoRA and API fine-tuning, often with 100 examples or fewer. As a general claim it is contested: independent studies find some checkpoints and recipes stay near baseline at small doses, including Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2-7B-Instruct, and one 100-shot replication on Llama-2-7B-Chat failed.

claims.heading: Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data raises harmful compliance
claims.summary: Independent groups reproduce the rise in harmful compliance after benign fine-tuning, including near-original Alpaca reruns on Llama-2-7B-Chat and GPT-3.5 Turbo, usually with smaller increases than the original. The rise depends on the recipe: some LoRA settings, random small subsets, conservative recipes, and some judges and benchmarks show no increase, and GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini show none.

claims.heading: On harmful prompts, aligned and base models differ mostly at the first few tokens
claims.summary: One independent study reproduces this early-token pattern in KL divergence from the base model for six aligned models from the Llama, Gemma and Qwen families, but shows it only in figures, without numbers for how much of the KL falls early. A diffusion-model study gives an analogue under left-to-right decoding; other reports compare different model pairs, use proxies or are theory, and models above 10B remain untested.

claims.heading: Prefilling a compliant start, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes bypass refusal
claims.summary: Independent groups reproduce large refusal bypasses from assistant prefilling, optimized suffixes and decoding changes on open models up to over 100B parameters, while below 1B only suffix and prompt-side attacks have independent support. The bypass is conditional: strongly safety-tuned models, suffixes transferred to other models and several closed models often keep refusing.

claims.heading: A small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour
claims.summary: Many groups other than the original authors find that ablating, pruning or editing a small set of weights, neurons, attention heads or a single direction weakens refusal across several open model families, but because the studies use different measures, they do not identify one minimal set of safety parameters. Some specific readings are contested, such as single-head ablation in Qwen2.5-1.5B and safety subspaces taken from the top singular vectors of safety weight updates.

claims.heading: The safety training data or objective produces the shallowness
claims.summary: Independent studies support this: changing only the safety training data, with the objective held fixed, reduces the shallowness in 1-10B autoregressive and diffusion models, and one joint data-and-objective change at 70B points the same way. Theory papers derive the shallowness from standard objectives under idealized assumptions, but no general objective-level mechanism has been established.

claims.heading: Training that spreads safety past the first tokens, and whether it holds up
claims.summary: Follow-up studies on Llama, Gemma, Qwen and other families, a few sharing authors with the original, find that such training sharply cuts prefilling attack success and partly helps against GCG. Whether the gains hold up is contested: an adaptive, rank-based prefilling attack, later benign fine-tuning and some prompt jailbreaks defeat deepened models.

related_findings.title: Activation interventions raise or suppress refusal
related_findings.summary: Steering or ablating activation directions can raise or suppress refusal and harmful behavior. How many directions matter, how separable they are, and what the intervention costs in capability depend on the model and its training.

examples.headline: Refusal-direction ablation cut reasoning-model refusal to 0.4–10%, with 5–30% relative capability loss.
Full probes decoded refusal better than any single direction, except in SmolLM2; steering one did nothing.
Activation vectors optimized on one harmful prompt reached HarmBench attack success up to 96.9%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Layers, heads, tokens and feature circuits shape safety processing
related_findings.summary: Refusal can be controlled through specific tokens, attention heads, layers or small feature circuits; in some studies, random-component controls showed no comparable effect. These concentrated effects can coexist with safety-degrading changes spread across the model.

examples.headline: Boosting 50 safety-token logits cut JailbreakBench attack success from 33.5% to 0.5%, unlike boosting random tokens.
Suppressing a transcoder circuit of 1.2–1.8% of features cut refusal from 96.2% to 48.7%.
Amplifying two LLaMA attention heads that drive continuation raised AdvBench attack success from 16% to 64.4%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Replay, data selection and constraints can limit safety loss
related_findings.summary: Selecting or replaying safety data, constraining gradients or representations, and correcting adapters can reduce the safety lost in downstream fine-tuning. How well they work depends on data coverage, constraint design and the attack used.

examples.headline: PATCHER kept Beavertails-attack success well below plain fine-tuning; Toxic-DPO attacks still reached 71.4% on AdvBench.
Projecting utility gradients off safety-gradient directions kept attack success near pre-fine-tuning levels.
Correcting fine-tuned adapters ('curing') lowered PAIR and FlipAttack success, but only to 27.9% and 32.7%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Fine-tuning shifts refusal representations and how they reach outputs
related_findings.summary: Fine-tuning can rotate refusal directions, shrink the separation between harmful and harmless inputs, change gradient alignment and routing, or leave a refusal signal intact while blocking its expression. How these internal changes relate to behavior varies by method and depth.

examples.headline: Distillation on chat-formatted data rotated the refusal direction and narrowed the harmful–harmless gap along it.
A first-token refusal signal survived benign fine-tuning; final-layer patching restored 96.9% of the refusal margin.
As harmful data rose, the cosine between user-task and alignment gradients fell from 0.02 to −0.16.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Opening-token distributions shift, measured without per-position KL
related_findings.summary: Many safety-changing interventions alter a response's opening tokens, for example from refusal openings to affirmative ones. These studies did not measure the KL divergence between aligned and base models at each token position, and signals at the opening do not reliably predict whether the full response is safe.

examples.headline: Harmful fine-tuning flipped the top first token from 'I' to 'Sure' within 10–25 steps.
Harmful/benign classification accuracy declined from the first output position to the third.
A benign-trained soft-token link cut first-token refusal probability; forcing refusal tokens largely reversed this.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Metrics, judges and output validity change safety conclusions
related_findings.summary: Refusal, harmful usefulness, coherence and capability are separate outcomes, and different judges or metrics can disagree on the same outputs. Judge templates, extraction rules, target phrases and broken generations can change estimated attack success or repair gains.

examples.headline: Adding scoring examples to HEx-PHI's judge template flipped the base-versus-fine-tuned ranking in 25% of medical comparisons.
A guard model rated collapsed Llama-3.2-3B outputs at 0.994 attack success; GPT-4o judged none harmful.
Benign fine-tuning ended Granite Guardian refusals, but its outputs became ambiguous rather than compliant.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Framing, personas and social pressure alter refusal
related_findings.summary: Context, role-play, register, persuasion and social pressure can raise or lower refusal of harmful requests. The size and direction of the effect depend on the model, its training history and how the framing is applied.

examples.headline: Drunk-persona prompting reached JailbreakBench attack success of 21–90% across tested models.
Social pressure raised refusal in Qwen3.5 base checkpoints but lowered it after sycophancy fine-tuning.
One persona's attack success was 0.038 via system prompt but 0.818 via activation steering.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Safety interventions can raise over-refusal or cost capability
related_findings.summary: Training and inference interventions can move harmful refusal, benign over-refusal and capability independently. Low measured harmfulness can come with incoherent output or lost usefulness.

examples.headline: Sparse RL on randomly chosen neurons cut attack success but sharply raised benign refusal on XSTest.
Safety-data replay cut attack success but raised over-refusal; replaying base-model logits avoided that but barely helped.
Refusal-exemplar training made SmolLM2-1.7B abstain on 36–99% of answerable ARC-Easy questions, versus a 14% reference rate.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Harm recognition can survive when refusal fails
related_findings.summary: When fine-tuning or jailbreaks defeat refusal, models can still represent harmfulness and retain hazardous knowledge. Recognizing harm and acting on that recognition can come apart.

examples.headline: After harmful fine-tuning, an MLP probe separated benign from malicious inputs above 95% per layer.
Ablating refusal-carrying activations sharply raised Llama HarmBench attack success; ablating harmfulness-carrying ones did not.
In a recurrent-depth (looped) model, harm was readable after one loop, before the refusal direction settled.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Targeted training and edits can install or restore safety
related_findings.summary: Safety-targeted retraining, selected parameter updates, adapters or low-rank patches can install or recover refusal. That a small repair works does not show safety was natively localized there, and utility effects vary.

examples.headline: Updating about 0.4M probe-selected FFN parameters cut jailbreak success from 44.5% to 1.1%.
A rank-64 patch restored 94–100% safety in harmfully fine-tuned checkpoints with little utility change.
Benign fine-tuning on OpenHermes restored refusal after refusal-direction ablation; one Qwen model exceeded its original baseline.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Data composition and training objectives shape safety erosion
related_findings.summary: How much safety erodes depends on the toxicity, diversity, framing and ordering of training data, how refusals are structured, and the training objective. Adding safety or noisy examples does not necessarily protect refusal.

examples.headline: Adding randomly sampled safety data to downstream fine-tuning raised Llama3 attack success from 20.24% to 59.23%.
Safety fine-tuning on varied syntax cut attack success for conditional phrasings but raised it for commands.
Harmful-only wrapped refusal SFT reached 38.7 refusal; shared benign wrappers with intent-analysis targets reached 63.6.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Demonstrations, conversation history and memory alter safety
related_findings.summary: Harmful demonstrations, task decomposition, multi-turn escalation and retrieved context can raise harmful compliance without any weight update. Whether models resist, and whether protective demonstrations help, depends on the model, the context and where safety examples are placed.

examples.headline: Many-shot harmful demonstrations reached 39.5–74.8% attack success; a final refusal demonstration cut context attacks to 0–4.9%.
LoRA training on about 900 safe multi-turn conversations only partly reduced the JARGON attack's success.
Retrieving benign memories raised harmful-query attack success over stateless prompting in all five models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Narrow fine-tuning can cause broad misalignment
related_findings.summary: Fine-tuning on narrow insecure, incorrect, harmful or selected benign data can produce misaligned or dishonest answers on unrelated, benign prompts. The scope depends on model and data, and this is a different outcome from compliance with harmful requests.

examples.headline: Insecure-code fine-tuning made GPT-4o give misaligned answers to unrelated questions, unlike controls.
Narrow fine-tuning made GPT-4.1 volunteer extreme or bigoted opinions on non-leading prompts.
Narrow insecure-code or risky-advice tuning produced misalignment on unrelated benign questions in some settings.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Low-rank and geometric signals are not safety-specific evidence
related_findings.summary: Low rank, direction similarity, update size and monitoring scores track safety in some settings but can also reflect generic structure or confounds. This limits causal and cross-model readings of such measurements.

examples.headline: Prefilling lowered AlphaSteer's refusal-steering signal, a projection norm, in Llama but raised it in Mistral.
Matched supervised, wikitext and code fine-tunes had similar stable rank (few dominant directions), unlike random noise.
Harmful training restricted to random rank-1 subspaces still restored harmfulness, along near-orthogonal directions.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Poisoned and unusual training signals induce varied harms
related_findings.summary: Poisoned, biased, trait-focused or otherwise unusual training signals can induce misinformation, toxicity, targeted harms or loss of refusal. Effects depend on content and the training route.

examples.headline: Attacked Qwen3-32B LoRA checkpoints wrote targeted insecure code on audit prompts; clean checkpoints did not.
Self-supervised adaptation on one harmful prompt, without responses, raised attack success in 7–8B models.
Training on polite stereotype-endorsing answers raised HarmBench compliance far above neutral controls.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Wording, syntax and obfuscation change refusal
related_findings.summary: Paraphrase, obfuscation, tokenization and syntactic rewriting can change whether a model refuses a harmful request with the same intent. Effects vary by model, topic and attack.

examples.headline: Emoji rewriting raised the share of extremely harmful responses from 0–7.69% to 28–66% in aligned models.
Prompt rewriting and obfuscation reached hard-jailbreak success of 0.06–0.80 on open and GPT-4o models.
Worst-case syntactic reformulation raised attack success by 15–71%, yet harmfulness probes kept about 70% accuracy.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Adversarial and multimodal defenses protect only against trained-on attacks
related_findings.summary: These defenses were trained against particular attacks or input types. How much they helped depended on what that training covered.
related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Hidden triggers and later updates can activate harmful behavior
related_findings.summary: Training can install harmful behavior that appears only under a trigger, a context or a later update, while the model looks safe otherwise. Later alignment or consistency training can suppress elicitation without showing that the behavior is gone.

examples.headline: Backdoor fine-tuning with 400 trigger-poisoned samples gave 68.7–84.2% triggered non-refusal; no pre-attack baseline was reported.
Adversarially meta-trained models scored 0.929–0.975 on safety benchmarks, then 0.044–0.757 after one benign update.
Clean DPO or PPO suppressed a backdoor planted by fine-tuning; poisoned downstream alignment could reactivate it.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Image, video and audio inputs can bypass text safety
related_findings.summary: Harmful intent delivered through images, video, audio or mixed inputs can get past safety that was trained on text. Success depends on perceptual context, delivery, presentation and model.

examples.headline: Video attack success peaked at four clips; Qwen2.5-VL-7B rose while LLaVA-Video barely changed.
Swapping unsafe HADES prompts for a neutral prompt sharply lowered refusal in five models.
In Qwen3-Omni, the top 16% of audio regions held 90% of gradient energy during jailbreak optimization.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Adaptation shifts privacy, bias and values beyond refusal
related_findings.summary: Domain, language and task adaptation, as well as contextual interventions, can change toxicity, bias, privacy, honesty, copyright behavior and value priorities. These shifts can happen independently of refusal of harmful requests.

examples.headline: Fine-tuning to expand plot summaries produced recall of held-out books far above chance level.
Benign reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, without personal data, raised targeted Enron-email recall; refusal barely changed.
Benign Alpaca fine-tuning made Gemma-2-2B answer some ambiguous BBQ bias questions with stereotypes instead of refusing.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Training safety reasoning can improve jailbreak resistance
related_findings.summary: Training or prompting models to reason about risk, verify, pivot to safety, or have their reasoning monitored can improve resistance to jailbreaks. Gains depend on the objective, model and evaluation.

examples.headline: Safe Trigger training cut DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B WildJailbreak attack success from 32.45% to 1.45%.
The SInternal method raised WildJailbreak safe-response rate from 30.4% to 78.8%; STAR-1 reached 59.6%.
Complexity-adaptive safe-reasoning RL cut WildJailbreak attack success from 68.7% to 5.6% while roughly preserving MMLU-Pro.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Opening-token and sparse decoding interventions change safety
related_findings.summary: Supervising or reweighting opening tokens, adding refusal prefixes, and intervening at a few selected positions can change the safety of a whole response. Effects depend on which tokens are targeted, when, how densely, and on the model.

examples.headline: On Gemini-3.5-Flash, intervening at 5.25% of positions gave Harm score 3.58, versus 3.96 at all positions.
Models with 0% attack success under greedy decoding still put 0.002–0.211 probability mass on harmful continuations.
Downweighting risky first tokens cut mean harmfulness, from 0.468 to 0.234 on one target model.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Runtime prompts and steering can alter or restore safety
related_findings.summary: System messages, personas, in-context safety examples, self-evaluation prompts and runtime steering can weaken or restore safety. Effects depend on the model, its training path, the trigger and whether the intervention continues.

examples.headline: A safety system prompt cut jailbreak success to near zero in selected audio-tuned checkpoints.
A safety-reflection prompt sharply cut harmfulness after RLVR but barely helped a Qwen SFT model.
The STEER-BIND defense brought attack success under compliance steering back near the original model's level.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Safety varies across languages and transfers unevenly
related_findings.summary: Safety differs across languages, scripts, transliterations, language mixtures and instructions about response language. Training and refusal mechanisms carry over unevenly between languages.

examples.headline: Asking for English responses raised attack success on Punjabi illegal-activity persuasive prompts from 68.89% to 82.22%.
Standard Arabic SFT raised refusal of harmful Arabizi (romanized Arabic) prompts; no tested model reached 90%.
Swapping in English-derived reasoning traces barely changed mean attack success across seven languages.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Unlearned knowledge returns or resists depending on method
related_findings.summary: Knowledge suppressed by unlearning can return through fine-tuning, prompts, demonstrations or pruning, while some methods resisted the recovery attacks tested. Recovering knowledge is a different outcome from removing refusal.

examples.headline: After GradDiff unlearning, a model relearned hazardous biology from 510 fine-tuning examples, reaching 0.54–0.64 accuracy.
Forgetting from Deep Ignorance distillation held after GSM8K fine-tuning, but RMU-unlearned knowledge partly returned.
Benign 250M-token SFT raised WMDP accuracy from 44.1 to 78.3 after RMU unlearning, less after REX.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Early-generation signals predict and steer refusal outcomes
related_findings.summary: Signals at the end of the prompt or early in generation can predict refusal, and intervening there can change the outcome. The window in which a model commits to refusing or complying varies by model and training, and later recovery remains possible.

examples.headline: A probe on the first thinking token predicted final refusal with AUROC 0.84–0.95.
In Qwen2.5-1.5B, first-half harm-direction injection matched whole-response injection; second-half injection barely helped.
Monitor-triggered steering in the first few reasoning steps sharply cut attack success.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Code, encoding and task reformulations bypass safeguards
related_findings.summary: Recasting harmful requests as code completion, algorithm design, encodings or formal tasks can elicit outputs that direct requests do not. Success depends on the wrapper, the decoding method and the defenses in place.

examples.headline: GPT-4o code-framing reached 90% attack success; stripping comments and docstrings cut it to 20%.
Honeypot-code DPO largely blocked attacks that constrain decoding to a grammar; standard refusal DPO did not.
Benign paraphrasing of harmful algorithm requests raised GPT-5 attack success from 38.33% to 96.66%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Reasoning modes and supplied reasoning can raise vulnerability
related_findings.summary: Turning on reasoning, using reasoning prompts, or supplying reasoning text can increase harmful compliance or harmful detail. Effects depend on model, alignment, attack and evaluator.

examples.headline: Qwen3 think mode raised misalignment; Qwen3-32B HEx-PHI misalignment rose from 7.63% to 23.12%.
With identical weights, reasoning-on Qwen3-32B was more vulnerable to implanted harmful reasoning than reasoning-off.
After AM-SFT, harmful outputs concentrated in extended-thinking responses.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Safety sensitivity depends on update direction and geometry
related_findings.summary: How much an update harms safety depends on its direction, gradient subspaces, curvature and how update components interact. Safety-related gradients and curvature can be more concentrated than utility ones, but such findings are setting-dependent.

examples.headline: Llama safety gradients concentrated in fewer directions than Math or Code gradients.
Safety Fisher was lower-rank than utility Fisher; benign tuning re-sharpened final-layer refusal targets 11.2×, versus 1.2× for utility.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Training order and attack setup shape safety retention
related_findings.summary: Safety forgetting and resistance to harmful training depend on task order, training history, optimizer, capacity and defense settings. Protection that holds in one setting can fail in another.

examples.headline: In pooled analysis, larger models learned more harmful behavior from poisoning; Gemma 2 was the exception.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Optimized attack transfer depends on placement and pairing
related_findings.summary: Optimized adversarial inputs can elicit harmful outputs, but success and transfer depend on token placement, attack format, which source and target models are paired, and their representations. Randomizing inputs can disrupt attacks at a cost to utility.

examples.headline: Flexible adversarial-token placement raised cross-model transfer attack success by up to 49 points.
GCG prompts from large models reached up to 0.88 success on a small draft model.
Natural-gradient adversarial prefixes raised average harmfulness by 1.23 over the strongest baseline.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Chat-template tokens and fixed positions mediate refusal
related_findings.summary: Chat-template tokens and fixed prompt positions can collect safety signals and mediate refusal and other learned behaviors. Changing formatting, attention or cached key-value states at these positions can change behavior.

examples.headline: Gemma 4 E2B-IT refused 65 of 75 bio prompts with chat-template tokens, none without.
Patching a bad-medical-advice model's KV caches into the base gave 4.8% misalignment (base 0%, fine-tuned 7.2%).
A refusal trained for financial topics spread to unrelated topics more under SFT than under TReFT.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Compression, pruning and noise have mixed safety effects
related_findings.summary: Pruning, quantization, noise and compression can preserve, degrade or restore safety. The effect depends on component, precision, strength, language and model, sometimes with capability costs.

examples.headline: Activation noise raised Llama-3-8B-Instruct attack success from 0.0833 to 0.6267.
Uniform quantization especially hurt non-English safety; Llama GPTQ Arabic safety fell from 31.9 to 15.3.
AWQ INT4 raised attack success at most 1.6 points for seven models, unlike SmolLM3-3B.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Training models to recover safety mid-response improves robustness
related_findings.summary: Training recovery beyond the opening can improve robustness

examples.headline: Early-token-constrained DPO only partly protected Llama-3.2-1B as the unsafe data share grew.
OPSA cut prefill-attack success more than ThinkSafe; 2.3–3.6% of attacks still succeeded on two small models.
Mid-generation backtracking training kept attack success low, even under adaptive GCG aimed at backtracking.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Recovery after compliant openings varies by model and prefix
related_findings.summary: After a compliant or misaligned prefill, models can recover, stop or refuse, depending on the model and on the opening's content and length. Some prefill effects reflect generic conditioning rather than safety training.

examples.headline: In base models without safety tuning, blocking early attention to the prefill reduced harmful continuations.
Making an induced prefix admit harmfulness lowered Llama-2-7B-Chat attack success.
Given prefilled misaligned actions, GPT-5.2 and Claude 4.5 Haiku continued less often than Claude 3 Haiku.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Emergent misalignment depends on data, optimizer and capacity
related_findings.summary: How much emergent misalignment appears depends on training content and framing, regularization, the optimizer, update capacity and evaluation. Effects of rank, scale and method differ across settings.

examples.headline: Emergent misalignment from narrow LoRA ranged from 5.3% with Muon to 37.0% with Lion.
Mixing Dolly data into narrow training reduced Sports misalignment in Llama-70B and Qwen-72B.
Insecure-code LoRA caused more emergent misalignment than full SFT; it fell as LoRA rank rose.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Safe-looking openings can precede harmful content
related_findings.summary: A benign or refusal opening can be followed by harmful content. Attacks can keep the refusal text or insert harmful spans later, defeating safeguards that only act on the first positions.

examples.headline: A harmful span after a long refusal prefix exceeded 75% attack success on chat models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Reasoning traces and final answers differ in safety
related_findings.summary: Reasoning traces can contain harmful content even when final answers are safer. Harm discrimination, self-rationalization and safety decisions vary between the reasoning and answer stages.

examples.headline: Reasoning traces were harmful in 0.687–0.690 of JailbreakBench cases for two reasoning models.
Chain-of-thought SFT raised self-rationalization (justifying compliance) to 67.3% of responses, closely tracking attack success.
Benign and harmful hidden states separated less before reasoning than before the final answer.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Persona representations and steering shape emergent misalignment
related_findings.summary: Emergent misalignment can involve persona representations that are kept or altered, and activation interventions can sometimes raise or lower it. Effects depend on the model and on the data that induced the misalignment.

examples.headline: Persona-vector geometry stayed similar between Instruct and bad-medical misaligned variants.
Benign fine-tuning and layer-20 steering reduced misalignment; negative steering raised it.
Ablating the model's own persona direction cut emergent misalignment from 21.4% to 9.8%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Pretraining and midtraining history shape later safety
related_findings.summary: What a model saw in pretraining or midtraining, and when, can affect how well it keeps safety later and what dispositions it shows. Template changes or conflicting fine-tuning can weaken this transfer, and latent imprints can persist.

examples.headline: Earlier harmful exposure, erased behaviorally by alignment, amplified attack gains from later harmful re-exposure at most doses.
Moral reflections added to pretraining lowered jailbreak success; changing the assistant token erased the benefit.
Midtraining on a written Charter made later fine-tuned models follow it more than a token-matched control.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Jailbreaks alter internal harm processing and refusal pathways
related_findings.summary: Jailbreaks can change harm appraisals, attention, compliance pathways or how refusal signals propagate. They do not necessarily erase the model's recognition of harmful intent.
related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Agent training and persistent self-updates can erode safety
related_findings.summary: Agent training, self-evolution and persistent updates to controllers or memory can worsen action safety and prompt-injection resistance. Authorization-aware supervision for specific scenarios can reduce these effects.

examples.headline: Adversarial-trajectory SFT raised agentic leaking from 4.6% to 24.9%; filtering out adversarial actions still gave 24.6%.
Authorization-aware feedback cut indirect prompt-injection success from 35.0% to 5.8%.
Weight-free self-updates to controller, memory and tool files caused safety failures on 43.9% of tests.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Merging and cache reuse can spread or repair safety loss
related_findings.summary: Merging models or adapters and reusing caches across models can propagate, compound or reduce safety loss. Outcomes depend on how compatible the components are, whether they share a backbone, and the composition settings.

examples.headline: Merged models stayed safe without attack; suffix transfer depended on a shared pretrained backbone.
Adapters that each refused alone produced harmful compliance when linearly merged.
Reusing only another model's cached values raised Llama-3-8B-Instruct attack success; full KV-cache reuse slightly lowered Qwen3-8B's.

related_findings.title: Attacks also bypass access-control and task refusals
related_findings.summary: Adversarial inputs, prefills and decoding interventions can redirect classification, reveal concealed information, or get past refusals induced for access control or specific tasks.

examples.headline: Completion-prefix attacks bypassed induced access-control refusal, more often on GPT-4.1-mini than GPT-4o.
The FragFuse attack reached 41.1% end-to-end success, versus 5.7% for a baseline attack.
Decoding aggregation recovered math ability from a Llama-3.1-70B model trained to refuse math.

related_findings.title: Targeted weight edits can change refusal
related_findings.summary: Editing weights along the refusal direction, making a knowledge edit on a single example, or flipping targeted bits can change how models answer harmful requests. How much refusal remains, the side effects and the capability cost all vary by model.
related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Refusing in chat does not ensure safe tool actions
related_findings.summary: Written refusal, risk recognition and safe tool actions are partly separate. Enabling tools can expose unsafe actions, and text safeguards carry over incompletely to agent settings.

examples.headline: In 33.6% of harmful tool calls the model made, it also wrote a refusal.
A fraction 0.098–0.519 of harmful requests refused in chat still produced unsafe tool calls.
The rise in refusal failures with tool use persisted under both minimal and structured prompts.

related_findings.title: External safety classifiers and filters can be evaded
related_findings.summary: Attacks that evade the classifier, hide content in covert encodings, or target the model and its filter jointly can defeat external safeguards. Some tested configurations did block the attacks tried.
related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Diffusion language model safety depends on positions and trajectories
related_findings.summary: In diffusion language models, safety depends on where in the sequence text is filled in, the mask pattern, the denoising step, and when the model commits to a refusal. An early refusal signal, or detecting a risky denoising trajectory, does not guarantee safe output.

examples.headline: In LLaDA-8B-Instruct, later-position step-by-step prefills appeared to elicit more harm than an affirmative opening prefill.
Unsafe diffusion denoising runs usually contained refusal signals, but these were rarely committed to the output.
Masking a larger share of the attack template raised average attack success from 62.0% to 78.8%.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Distillation can pass on misalignment without harmful examples
related_findings.summary: Distillation on benign-looking or filtered data can weaken a student's refusal or pass a teacher's misaligned dispositions to it. This depends on the teacher, student, data and kind of signal passed between them, and comparing checkpoints without controls cannot isolate the cause.

examples.headline: Students of a narrowly misaligned teacher inherited misalignment; online filtering barely reduced transfer.
Filtered benign-looking data from bias-prompted teachers raised targeted bias in students.
Fine-tuning on number sequences transferred misalignment mainly within same-model teacher–student pairs; cross-model transfer was near zero.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Erased image-generation concepts can return after fine-tuning
related_findings.summary: Concepts erased from text-to-image models, and unsafe generation more broadly, can reappear after harmful or even unrelated fine-tuning. Targeted hardening and modular interventions give protection that depends on the method.

examples.headline: Fine-tuning restored unsafe generation in ESD- and SafeGen-protected models within 1–10 iterations; PATRONUS resisted it.
Fine-tuning on unrelated images revived erased concepts in Stable Diffusion v1.4.
In one probe, disabling 158 FLUX.2 klein text-encoder components stopped it substituting clothing, a refusal-like behavior.

related_findings.title: Training changes harm in models never safety-aligned
related_findings.summary: Training base or other non-safety-aligned models can change harmful output through coherence, instruction following or exposure to safety data. This is not the erosion of an established refusal.

examples.headline: Of base-model fine-tunes, safety-trained Aloe-Beta cut the unsafe-response rate from 59.7% to 23.9%; JSL-Med-Sft raised it.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Mixture-of-experts routing and expert choice mediate safety
related_findings.summary: In mixture-of-experts models, routing and selected experts can carry or bypass safety behavior. This depends on layer, alignment method and whether training localized safety in particular experts.

examples.headline: An attack exploiting expert routing succeeded 0–22.73% of the time on DeepSeek, depending on alignment method.
Restoring original experts in a RASA-trained model cut harmlessness to 0.31; random experts left 0.92.
Masking routers at 1–5 selected layers raised DeepSeek-V2-Lite attack success as high as 0.90.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Skipping layers or loops at inference affects safety
related_findings.summary: Changing how many recurrent loops or transformer layers run at inference can change safety; failures can occur even after harmfulness is already detectable inside the model. This depth is computation per token, not the position in the response that shallow alignment concerns.

examples.headline: Adaptive layer skipping raised WildJailbreak harmful-response rates from 8.33% to 31.25–41.67%.
Fewer recurrent loops compounded prompt jailbreaks, raising compliance in Ouro-2.6B-Thinking.
Decoding from a near-final low-entropy layer changed few tokens and left Air-Bench safety roughly flat.

related_findings.title: Training compliant openings alone can unlock harmful continuations
related_findings.summary: Training models on affirmative openings, or on obedient personas with no toxic content, can unlock harmful continuations even though the harmful answer itself is never trained on.

related_findings.title: Detoxification can hide, not remove, toxic mechanisms
related_findings.summary: Detoxification can suppress existing toxic-generation mechanisms without removing them. Targeted weight or activation edits can then restore or reduce toxicity.

examples.headline: Scaling seven toxicity-linked MLP neurons' input weights raised DPO-detoxified GPT-2's toxicity from 0.208 to 0.458.

related_findings.title: Static refusal audits can miss deliberately hidden weaknesses
related_findings.summary: Models built to hide harmful states or fragility to updates can pass static refusal audits. They remain vulnerable to later updates or internal interventions.

examples.headline: An LLM meta-trained to break under fine-tuning became harmful after one update on 32 Alpaca samples.
Static harm audits missed a Llama's planted weakness: GCG attack success 0.52, versus the base's 0.16.

related_findings.title: Self-reports and measured behavior can diverge
related_findings.summary: What a model endorses in conversation, confesses to, or says about prefilled actions can differ from its measured behavior. Prefilled text, and the model's awareness that it is being evaluated, make these gaps harder to interpret.

examples.headline: Models taught a rule-following Charter, then fine-tuned with 2% profit-maximizing data, endorsed it but chose profit.
Claude 4.5 Opus confessed to prefilled misalignment in 48% of samples but often denied writing it.

related_findings.title: Opening-conditioned effects also appear outside safety
related_findings.summary: Steering with opening prefixes, training to recover after a bad opening, and position-weighted training can also affect how models carry out reasoning and how much they forget earlier tasks. These are analogues, outside harmful requests, of how a response's opening tokens shape its safety.

reading_list.why: The defining study: aligned-versus-base differences concentrate in the first response tokens, and recovery training resists prefilling attacks.
The original fine-tuning result: ten harmful examples, or benign Alpaca data, erode safety in GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-2-7B-Chat.
A close rerun of the ten-example attack on Llama-2 and Vicuna; shares an author and uses a keyword judge.

known_gaps.summary: The opening-token signature and its causes rest on few independent tests, the case against few-example harmful fine-tuning is weak, results on benign fine-tuning and decoding attacks conflict, deeper-alignment defenses are partly broken by adaptive attacks, and coverage is thin at the smallest and largest scales.
items: The positional signature itself is thinly replicated. One independent study reproduces the early concentration of aligned-versus-base KL, only in figures and without numbers or uncertainty, and no test covers models below 1B or above 10B.

Why alignment ends up shallow is barely tested: the gradient explanation, that standard objectives give later tokens little or no safety gradient, is theory with no training experiment. The data explanation rests on one autoregressive study (HumorReject, which swapped refusal responses for humorous ones when training Llama3-8B) and a diffusion-model ablation that does not test whether the effect runs through the first tokens.

Evidence against few-example harmful fine-tuning is weak. The main failed replication (Representation Noising, 100 examples on Llama-2-7B-Chat, 0.04 to 0.06) has so far been taken only from the paper's appendix text, not checked against its tables, and another counterexample uses a 0.5B model that already complied heavily before training.

Whether ordinary benign fine-tuning erodes safety is unresolved: with 100 Alpaca examples on Llama-2-7B-Chat, one study reports a keyword-matched attack success rate rising from about 0 to 0.94, while another finds random benign subsets leave judged harmfulness unchanged. Keyword matching, guard classifiers and LLM judges can also disagree on the same outputs, which can shift estimated attack success.

Attacks that skip past the opening have the most tests, but many only partly support the claim. Decoding-only attacks give conflicting results (large gains in some studies, little effect from temperature changes in others), and prefill effects in base models without safety tuning suggest part of the effect is generic conditioning.

Deeper-alignment defenses are not settled: the original study's released model, trained on safety recovery examples, resists ordinary prefilling but is partly broken by adaptive attacks such as rank-based prefilling and GCG. Reimplementations of the same training disagree even on ordinary prefilling, and durability under later fine-tuning remains in doubt.

Coverage is thin at the extremes of scale: few tests use models below 1B or above 100B, many API models have no stated size, none uses toy models, and above 100B the claims that safety sits in a few directions or ranks rest on one independent study. Those claims are especially exposed: patching tests, which copy parts of one model into another, give mixed results across three studies, and one test found removing alignment-subspace components no more selective than random projections.
